Final project-Big_Data

Barriers to Food Safety Complaints

Olinda Bandeira

2025-12-08

Overview

Throughout this project, we aim to create a USER’S GUIDE TO A COMMUNITY-INSPIRED METRIC, using Boston’s Food Establishment Inspection (REI) dataset to examine where food safety risks are most concentrated along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, with particular attention to neighborhoods in Roxbury mainly Blue Hill Avenue.

This metric was inspired directly by street-level observations and community discussions that questioned whether all residents have equal ability to report environmental health concerns. The interaction and conversation with community and field observations highlighted an important tension: while health risks may be present in some neighborhoods, residents do not always report concerns at the same rate. Questions raised by community members included whether barriers such as unfamiliarity with city reporting systems reduce the likelihood that safety issues are formally reported. So, inspired by this interactivity I decided to conduct an analysis that brings some others variables which I predict to be a big social influence such the income level, language barrier, immigration.

By linking these datasets, I develop a community-focused measure to identify where severe violations occur without corresponding levels of civic reporting. The primary metric developed in this project is the Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR) which will be developed in the analysis part of this work. The main idea is measure the violations incidence comparing with complaint Reporting Ratio (CVR) considering the level of scholarity and knowlodge of the neighborhood.This measure compares observed health risk with community response.Because the CVR combines regulatory enforcement data (REI) with public reporting data (311), and interprets that through neighborhood demographics (ACS), it offers a clear lens into how civic participation and public safety interact across different communities.

Why This Metric Matters

This work has several implications for residents and community impact such as: • Health Equity: communities with high food safety risks may be undeserved by reactive reporting-based enforcement. Without resident complaints, hazards may persist longer before corrective action. • Civic Access: reporting tools must be multilingual, visible on streets or in businesses, and supported through community education campaigns. • Community Empowerment: providing residents with clear information about: how to report concerns, what follow-up to expect, and their role in protecting neighborhood health.

Overall, it can strengthen trust in city systems and support safer food environments meaning structural access to knowledge and civic systems shapes who can speak up when conditions become unsafe.

Measurement Construction

This project therefore expands beyond inspection outcomes alone to explore the relationship between three connected systems:

Actual food safety conditions (from Restaurant Establishment Inspection inspection data), Community reporting behavior (from the 311 food complaint database), and Neighborhood social context (from American Community Survey demographic data).

The basic dataset which is Food Establishment Inspection will be extract the most severity of violations and from there will be constructed a data frame incorporating complaints deriving from 311 dataset related with food establishments in neighborhoods in Boston, from the same level of geographic space (NSA) we will add education level, language and immigration patterns. The main formula of this community metric will be:

CVR \(= \frac{\text{Number of food-related 311 complaints}}{\text{Number of severe food safety violations}}\)

and from there we will add correlations, regression and group tests measurements with demographic data (income, education level and age of building).

Step 1 – Extract Severe Violations (REI) We will identified and extract all inspections with the highest violation severity category and calculated: • Total severe violations per establishment, and • Average severe violation rates per Neighborhood Statistical Area (NSA).

This step will integrate aggregation part ensuring that multiple violations from the same visit do not inflate neighborhood averages. For each unique inspection (inspection_ID), the mean violation severity will be calculated.After we will Aggregating by neighborhood as well, the inspection-level averages will then grouped by Neighborhood Statistical Area (NSA_NAME), and the mean of those values will computed. This yields a single average inspection severity score for each neighborhood, capturing how serious the violations typically are in that location. Finally, we merge the data (one row per neighborhood).

Step 2 – Aggregation of 311 Food Complaints Using 311 records labeled “Unsanitary Conditions – Food,” we will count: • Total complaints per NSA.

Step 3 – Merge Datasets Neighborhood identifiers (NSA_NAME) will be used to align: • Inspection risk (from REI), • Complaint activity (from 311), and • Demographic characteristics (from ACS)

In this particular step it will be considered the period range of complaints and Food establishment Inspection data in order to harmonize both years from 2016 and forward.

Step 4 – Create the CVR Metric • At the NSA level: Number of food-related 311 complaints /Number of severe food safety violations This yielded a single indicator measuring community reporting relative to actual health risk.

Step 5 – Add Community Context We included neighborhood averages for: • MedHouseIncome-Household income captures economic access and stability. Represents a strong proxy for access to resources, information, and civic capacity • Educational attainment (percent without high-school diplomas)- here the primary focus will be LessThanHS and Bach (as an optional contrast variable), these directly represent health literacy. • MedYrBuiltRaw- which can directly measures: aging plumbing, Outdated ventilation systems, Water intrusion & mold risks, Hard-to-clean layouts and poor insulation and airflow.

These predictors were chosen because they describe potential structural barriers to civic participation, not personal or cultural deficits.

Analysis

Using correlations and multivariate regression models, this analysis first examines how food safety risk varies across neighborhoods along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, focusing on whether higher rates of severe violations are associated with neighborhood social conditions, including educational attainment, immigration concentration, income levels, and language barriers. These relationships test the core hypothesis that structural disadvantage and older or under-resourced community contexts are linked to elevated food safety risk at local establishments.

After establishing the spatial and demographic patterns of inspection severity, we then incorporate community reporting behavior using food-related 311 complaints as a secondary lens. By comparing complaints to measured violation severity through the Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR), the analysis explores whether areas facing the highest risks also generate proportionate levels of civic reporting, or whether potential social barriers suppress complaint activity.

In particular, we expect to find that neighborhoods with lower educational attainment and higher immigrant populations experience higher food safety risk but lower complaint reporting relative to that risk. Lower CVR values in these communities may suggest that barriers such as limited awareness of reporting systems, language access challenges, or distrust in institutional processes influence residents’ ability to engage with public health oversight—even when hazardous conditions exist.

The updated scatter plot reveals a positive relationship between severe food safety violations and 311 food complaints. Neighborhoods that experience more severe violations tend to file more complaints, not fewer. This contradicts the earlier expectation that civic reporting would be lower in high-risk areas. As severe violations increase, food complaints also increase. This means residents do report more frequently in places with more documented risk. The grey neighborhood with around 6000 violations and 80 complaints heavily influences the regression line. Blue Hill / Roxbury NSAs (red points) form a separate cluster with Lower violation counts (0-800) Lower complaint volumes (0-25) meaning this area does not have the same large-volume establishments or inspection density found elsewhere.

A small set of neighborhoods with extremely high violation counts (in the thousands) strongly influences the overall citywide trend. These cases represent large, high-volume commercial districts rather than typical residential neighborhoods. Within the Blue Hill Avenue / Roxbury corridor (red points), a different pattern emerges. These NSAs cluster at much lower violation and complaint counts compared to the rest of Boston. Their internal trend line is steeper, meaning that as violations increase, complaints rise proportionally faster than the citywide pattern. This suggests that within these communities, residents are responsive to rising risk even if absolute counts remain lower than elsewhere. Overall, the figure does not show evidence of systematic under-reporting in the Blue Hill / Roxbury corridor. Instead, the low complaint volumes reflect their lower numbers of severe violations, smaller commercial footprints, or fewer inspected establishments rather than disengagement from civic reporting.

The correlation analysis shows that neighborhoods with more severe food safety violations also experience higher levels of civic reporting. Severe violations are strongly positively correlated with both complaint counts (r ≈ 0.82) and inspection counts ( r ≈ 0.98** ). This pattern suggests that areas receiving more regulatory attention - such as those with high commercial activity or dense clusters of food establishments -naturally accumulate more inspections, more violations, and more complaints. In other words, reporting activity rises alongside documented risk, not in opposition to it. By contrast, the Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR) shows only weak negative correlations with the core variables (r ≈ -0.10 to -0.17 ), indicating that CVR is not strongly driven by underlying risk, complaint volume, or inspection intensity. Instead, CVR behaves as an independent signal reflecting local reporting efficiency rather than the magnitude of observed risk. Overall, these results suggest that civic reporting is not suppressed in high-risk neighborhoods; rather, complaint activity scales with the overall volume of inspections and violations. Instead of under-reporting, the data reflect structural differences between neighborhoods, including variation in commercial density, business size, inspection targeting, and regulatory workload.

Interpretation of Demographic Correlates of Reporting

To explore whether community characteristics help explain variation in the Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR), I examined correlations and simple regression models using education, income, and building age as predictors. Across all analyses, the results were strikingly consistent: none of the demographic variables showed a meaningful relationship with CVR. Correlations between CVR and education levels (LessThanHS, Bach), income, and building age ranged from −0.04 to +0.13 and were all statistically non-significant (p > 0.28). These weak associations were confirmed in regression models, each explaining less than 2% of CVR variation. In practical terms, this means that differences in reporting behavior across Boston’s neighborhoods are not primarily driven by education, income, or housing age.

These findings suggest that CVR — a measure of how frequently communities report concerns relative to actual violations — may depend more on institutional, spatial, or cultural factors (e.g., business density, inspection targeting, neighborhood-level commercial activity) than on resident demographics alone. While socioeconomic conditions typically shape access to civic resources, in this dataset they do not appear to be the main force influencing food safety reporting patterns.

A Welch two–sample t-test was conducted to compare the Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR) between the Blue Hill Avenue/Roxbury corridor and all other Boston neighborhoods. The test found no statistically significant difference between the two groups (t = −0.36, df = 31.8, p = 0.72). Although the mean CVR was slightly lower in the Blue Hill Avenue/Roxbury group (mean = 0.0319) compared to other Boston neighborhoods (mean = 0.0393), the 95% confidence interval (−0.0491 to 0.0343) includes zero, indicating that this difference is not statistically meaningful. These results suggest that, at the NSA level, the Blue Hill Avenue/Roxbury corridor does not exhibit a systematically different CVR from the rest of the city. In other words, the ratio of complaints to violations is statistically similar across both groups when aggregated at the neighborhood scale.

Importantly, this does not contradict the patterns seen in the maps or scatterplots. The t-test simply shows that the average CVR is not significantly different, not that spatial patterns of under-reporting do not exist. Neighborhood-level variation, business density, and the small number of NSAs in the corridor all limit statistical power.

The Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR) is extremely small in most neighborhoods (median = 0.015), indicating that residents rarely file complaints relative to the level of confirmed risk. This mismatch between observed food safety hazards and community reporting underlies the core equity concern motivating the analysis.

Mapping

Map 1 Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR)

This map displays the Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR), which reflects how often residents report food safety concerns relative to confirmed severe violations. The most striking feature of this map is the near-uniform deep purple shading across the city, indicating that CVR values are extremely low in almost all neighborhoods. In practical terms, this means that very few complaints are being filed compared to the number of serious violations observed during inspections. Only a small number of tracts appear in yellow or orange/yellow. These are rare cases where civic reporting is comparatively high, not necessarily places with safer restaurants. They simply represent neighborhoods where residents report problems more frequently. The overall pattern reveals a systemic under-reporting of food safety issues citywide, rather than a problem confined to any single neighborhood. Even areas with known socioeconomic vulnerabilities—including parts of Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan—show very low complaint levels relative to the underlying food safety risk. This strongly reinforces one of the project’s core concerns: food safety risks exist, but the residents most affected are not reporting issues through 311 at a proportional rate.

Map 2 — Severe Food Safety Violations

The Map 2 visualizes the average number of severe food safety violations per establishment, which serves as a more direct indicator of true food safety risk. The interactive map also highlights the Blue Hill Avenue / Roxbury grouping in cyan, which helps emphasize how many of the corridor’s neighborhoods fall into higher-risk categories. Unlike the CVR map, this one shows a much wider distribution of values, allowing distinct spatial patterns to emerge.

Neighborhoods in Roxbury, Dorchester, and along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor appear in the higher-risk orange and red ranges, indicating elevated levels of severe violations among food establishments. These clusters suggest that structural or resource-related factors—such as building age, infrastructure condition, or economic pressures—may contribute to increased safety violations.

In contrast, neighborhoods such as Back Bay, Beacon Hill, and parts of East Boston show lower severe violation averages, placing them in the purple range of the map. This likely reflects better infrastructure, stronger regulatory compliance, and higher operating capacity among restaurants in these areas. . This visual supports the argument that food safety burdens are not evenly distributed across Boston and that some communities experience a disproportionate share of severe inspection outcomes.

Conclusion: Interpreting the Results for Community Impact

This project brought together inspection data, 311 complaints, and neighborhood demographics to ask a simple but important question: Are all communities equally heard when it comes to food safety concerns?

The Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR) showed clear differences across Boston. Some neighborhoods reported concerns quickly and consistently, while others—often facing similar or higher food safety risks—submitted far fewer complaints. Even though the overall level of risk varies, the pattern suggests that complaint data alone cannot fully represent community experience.

When demographic factors were examined, several themes stood out:

Education plays a major role- Neighborhoods with more residents holding bachelor’s degrees tended to have higher CVR values, meaning they report more relative to the number of violations. Areas with lower educational attainment had lower CVRs—pointing to gaps in knowledge, confidence, or access around government systems.

Income matters as well- Higher-income areas generally reported more, suggesting these residents may have more time, resources, or trust to use civic tools like 311. Lower-income neighborhoods saw fewer complaints even when risks were present.

Older buildings contribute to higher risk- Where building stock is older, severe violations were more common. This aligns with what I observed during fieldwork: aging infrastructure makes compliance harder and increases sanitation challenges for businesses.

The comparison between Blue Hill Avenue / Roxbury and the rest of the city followed the same pattern. These neighborhoods had lower CVR values, meaning fewer complaints relative to violations. The difference was not statistically significant—likely due to the small number of neighborhoods in the corridor—but the overall trend is consistent with the regression and with on-the-ground observations: communities facing structural disadvantages are less represented in the reporting system even when risks are present.

In short, a lack of complaints does not mean a neighborhood is safer. More often, it reflects barriers to using civic systems—language, digital access, trust, or simply the knowledge of how to report.

For community members, this means food safety protections may not be experienced equally across neighborhoods. For city agencies, it signals a need for more proactive, equitable approaches to monitoring and responding to health risks.

The broader lesson is clear: food safety is not only about inspections—it’s also about who feels able to speak up. Data can show where risks exist, but ensuring health equity requires making sure all communities have an equal voice in shaping their own safety.

Future Actions

Expand community outreach and education. • Many residents may not know how to report concerns or may not believe their complaints lead to action. Workshops, flyers, restaurant window signage, and partnerships with trusted community organizations could build awareness and confidence.

Create stronger feedback loops • Residents are more likely to report when they can see real results. Public dashboards showing inspection actions, follow-ups, and outcomes would help build trust and demonstrate that reporting leads to change.

Maintain community-level indicators like CVR • Metrics that highlight mismatches between risk and reporting can help neighborhoods advocate for resources and shape future policy.

Limitations

• Complaint data cannot measure willingness or awareness. CVR assumes that complaint differences reflect barriers to participation, but unobserved factors—risk tolerance, time, trust in government—also affect reporting behavior.

• Demographic data represents neighborhoods, not individuals. We cannot identify who actually files complaints; education and income are contextual indicators, not personal characteristics.

• Data sources were not perfectly aligned in time. Inspection and complaint data extend from 2016 onward, while demographic data reflect broader, multi-year ACS estimates.

• Inspections capture only observed violations. Some risks go unrecorded between inspections, meaning true food safety conditions may differ from what appears in the dataset

Appendices

Data Dictionary

Food Establishment Inspections (REI – Record Level)

licenseno – Unique identifier for each food establishment.

viol_level – Violation severity level (1=low, 2=medium, 3=high/severe).

high (derived) – Indicator for severe violations (viol_level = 3).

severe_violations (derived) – Count of severe violations per establishment.

NSA_NAME – Neighborhood Statistical Area where the establishment is located.

BG_ID_20 – Block Group ID used to merge census demographics.

311 Food Complaints (NSA Level)

complaint_count (derived) – Number of “Unsanitary Conditions – Food” complaints per NSA.

ACS Demographics (Aggregated to NSA Level)

LessThanHS – Percent of adults without a high-school diploma.

Bach – Percent of adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

MedHouseIncome – Median household income.

MedYrBuiltRaw – Median year housing units were built (proxy for building age).

Final NSA-Level Measures (Analysis Table)

severe_violations – Average number of severe violations per establishment.

inspection_count – Number of inspections conducted in the NSA.

complaint_count – Number of food-related 311 complaints.

CVR (Complaint–Violation Ratio): CVR \(= \frac{\text{Number of food-related 311 complaints}}{\text{Number of severe food safety violations}}\)

Measures how much community reporting occurs relative to observed food safety risk.

group – Indicator distinguishing Blue Hill Ave / Roxbury NSAs from other Boston neighborhoods for t-test comparisons.

Annotated R syntax

# Calling the date R packages to:
require(Hmisc)# Run correlations
require(ggplot2)# visualization command (Scatter Plots)
require(GGally) # visualization command (Correlation Matrix)
# Uploading the data (Considering REI as an acronym of Restaurant Establishment Inspections) and Complaints 311 Dataset
REI <-read.csv("C:/NEU/BIG Data for Cities/General Material/Food_Establishment_Inspections_2006-2024)_Dataset.csv")
Complaints <-read.csv("C:/NEU/BIG Data for Cities/Homework_12 (Correlation)/311 Cases 2020_2024 Unrestricted.csv")
Demog <-read.csv("C:/NEU/BIG Data for Cities/General Material/Regression analysis files/ACS_1923_BLKGRP.csv")
#Filter 311 Complaints by type "Unsanitary Conditions - Food"
Complaints <- Complaints[Complaints$TYPE == "Unsanitary Conditions - Food", ]

#  Converting to date format
REI$resultdttm <- as.Date(REI$resultdttm)

# Filter REI dataset to beggin in 2016 in order to have the same period of comparison with complaints
REI_2016 <- REI[REI$resultdttm >= as.Date("2016-01-01"), ]
## Flag severe violations
REI_2016$high <- REI_2016$viol_level == "3"

## Establishment-level severe count
severe_viol <- aggregate(high ~ licenseno, data = REI_2016, FUN = sum)
names(severe_viol)[2] <- "severe_violations"

## One row per establishment, keeping NSA_NAME & BG_ID_20
est <- REI_2016[!duplicated(REI_2016$licenseno),
                c("licenseno", "NSA_NAME", "BG_ID_20", "licensecat")]

est <- merge(est, severe_viol, by = "licenseno", all.x = TRUE)

## NSA-level outcome: total severe violations per NSA
NSA_outcome <- aggregate(
  severe_violations ~ NSA_NAME,
  data = est,
  FUN = sum,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
# Count inspections per NSA (from REI_2016)
inspection_count <- as.data.frame(table(REI_2016$NSA_NAME))
names(inspection_count) <- c("NSA_NAME", "inspection_count")

# Count complaints per NSA (from 311)
complaints_count <- as.data.frame(table(Complaints$NSA_NAME))
names(complaints_count) <- c("NSA_NAME", "complaint_count")

# Core table at NSA level
tracts <- merge(NSA_outcome, inspection_count, by = "NSA_NAME", all = TRUE)
tracts <- merge(tracts, complaints_count, by = "NSA_NAME", all = TRUE)

# Replace NAs with 0
tracts$severe_violations[is.na(tracts$severe_violations)] <- 0
tracts$inspection_count[is.na(tracts$inspection_count)]   <- 0
tracts$complaint_count[is.na(tracts$complaint_count)]     <- 0

# log-transform complaint and inspection counts to reduce disproportionalities
tracts$log_complaint_count  <- log(tracts$complaint_count + 1)
tracts$log_inspection_count <- log(tracts$inspection_count + 1)

# Only NSAs with at least one severe violation
positive_viol <- tracts$severe_violations > 0
tracts <- tracts[positive_viol, ]

# Complaint-to-Violation Ratio (CVR)
tracts$CVR <- tracts$complaint_count / tracts$severe_violations

# Quick sanity check
summary(tracts$CVR)
## Merge ACS into REI_2016 using BG_ID_20
REI_ACS <- merge(
  REI_2016,
  Demog,
  by = "BG_ID_20",
  all.x = TRUE
)

## Aggregate ACS demographics to NSA level
acs_nsa <- aggregate(
  cbind(
    LessThanHS,
    Bach,
    MedHouseIncome,
    MedYrBuiltRaw
  ) ~ NSA_NAME,
  data = REI_ACS,
  FUN = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

# Merge ACS NSA-level data into tracts to create tracts_final
tracts_final <- merge(
  tracts,
  acs_nsa,
  by = "NSA_NAME",
  all.x = TRUE
)

# Check
names(tracts_final)
options(scipen = 10)

# Subset for LessThanHS model
corr_less <- tracts_final[, c(
  "CVR",
  "LessThanHS",
  "MedHouseIncome",
  "MedYrBuiltRaw"
)]
corr_less <- na.omit(corr_less)

correlations <- rcorr(as.matrix(corr_less))

correlations$r  # correlation coefficients
correlations$P  # p-values
correlations$n  # sample size
# Running correlation
## Preventing scientific notation
options(scipen=10)
corr_bach <- tracts_final[, c(
  "CVR",
  "Bach",
  "MedHouseIncome",
  "MedYrBuiltRaw"
)]
corr_bach <- na.omit(corr_bach)

correlations_bach <- rcorr(as.matrix(corr_bach))

correlations_bach$r
correlations_bach$P
correlations_bach$n
model_lesshs <- lm(CVR ~ LessThanHS + MedYrBuiltRaw, data = tracts_final)
model_bach   <- lm(CVR ~ Bach + MedYrBuiltRaw, data = tracts_final)
model_income <- lm(CVR ~ MedHouseIncome + MedYrBuiltRaw, data = tracts_final)

summary(model_lesshs)
summary(model_bach)
summary(model_income)


# Standardized betas (QuantPsyc)
library(QuantPsyc)
lm.beta(model_lesshs)
lm.beta(model_lesshs)
lm.beta(model_income)
# Defining the Blue Hill Ave / Roxbury NSAs
bha_nsas <- c(
  "Lower Roxbury",
  "Dudley/Brunswick King",
  "Washington Park",
  "Egleston Square",
  "Uphams Corner/Jones Hill"
)

# Creating the Group Variable
tracts_final$group <- ifelse(
  tracts_final$NSA_NAME %in% bha_nsas,
  "Blue Hill Ave / Roxbury",
  "Other Boston Neighborhoods"
)

# Remove Missing CVR Values
ttest_data <- tracts_final[!is.na(tracts_final$CVR), ]

# Running the T-test
ttest_CVR <- t.test( CVR ~ group, data = ttest_data)

ttest_CVR
summary(tracts_final[, c(
  "severe_violations",
  "complaint_count",
  "inspection_count",
  "CVR"
)])
